title: Ping penalty curation playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc collects bench notes, quick visualizations and a recommended operational playbook for the "ping penalty" phenomenon: the incremental latency and cost impact caused by tight client-side request pacing (very small inter-request gaps) interacting with server scheduling, batching, and prewarm heuristics. Intended audience: console/tooling, serving runtime, and SRE. Draft: experimental numbers, not yet prod-validated.

Background summary (TL;DR):
- When clients issue many tiny requests spaced by a few milliseconds, we often see worse p90/p99 latency and higher per-token cost than if the same tokens were sent in fewer, slightly larger requests. Causes: scheduling jitter, slot fragmentation, cold slot churn, and suboptimal packing (small batches map to underutilized GPU kernels).
- The trade-off surface is non-linear. Small increases in client-side batching time (10-30ms) can capture a large fraction of savings with marginal perceptual impact.

Experiment matrix (single-GPU, mixed short/long chat workload):
Scenarios tested: A) immediate-forward (no client-side buffering), B) 20ms client buffer, C) 50ms buffer, D) multiplex client (up to 8 concurrent streams per connection), E) aggressive prewarm (keep 1 idle slot warm per 100 active sessions).
All runs: 30-minute steady state, synthetic user mix 70% short-turn (<=40 tokens), 30% long-turn (200-600 tokens).

Summary table (aggregate numbers):
Scenario | median(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens (relative)
A: immediate | 64 | 212 | 880 | 230 | 1.00x
B: 20ms buffer | 68 | 138 | 360 | 285 | 0.82x
C: 50ms buffer | 75 | 120 | 270 | 330 | 0.74x
D: multiplex(8) | 70 | 150 | 380 | 320 | 0.78x
E: prewarm | 62 | 125 | 260 | 300 | 0.80x

Notes on numbers:
- Immediate mode (A) shows decent median but very large tail (p99). Tail is driven by slot churn and kernel underfill when many small requests arrive.
- 20ms buffer (B) reduces p95 dramatically; p99 improves by ~2.4x. Throughput rises because batching increases kernel efficiency. Cost per token improves ~18%.
- 50ms buffer (C) yields diminishing latency returns on median but best dollar-token ratio here: ~26% cost improvement vs immediate. For interactive UX, 50ms is borderline but acceptable for many chat UIs.
- Multiplexing (D) approximates buffering benefits without delaying the first byte, but it requires client-side complexity and different TCP connection semantics. Observed small increase in median due to head-of-line interactions but much lower p99 compared to immediate.
- Prewarm (E) is powerful when you can amortize a warm slot across sessions. It gives tail improvement close to buffering with lower client change required, costed by idle slot reservation.

Light ASCII visualization (p99 vs cost curve snapshot):
p99 latency (ms)   | Cost factor (1x = immediate)
900 +             | A(1.00)
700 - 900         | 
500 - 700         | D(0.78)
300 - 500         | B(0.82)
200 - 300         | E(0.80), C(0.74)
<200              | (sweet spot) C/E

Micro-observations and root causes found in traces:  
- Frequent tiny batches cause kernel launch overhead to dominate; we see high per-batch overhead in the first 10 tokens of long sequences (kernel startup + caching).
- Scheduler will sometimes assign tiny batches to new slots rather than packing into an existing slot if inter-arrival jitter > 12ms.
- HTTP chunking / response streaming increases p99 when combined with immediate-forward because streaming keeps connections active and prevents aggressive packing heuristics from consolidating requests.

Operational knobs we can expose (prioritized):
1) client_side_buffer_ms (default 25ms): small cross-client buffer implemented in SDKs and recommended for low-latency chat clients.
2) multiplexer_per_conn (default 4): allow SDK to multiplex logical sessions; useful for mobile/web where connection count is cheap.
3) prewarm_reservation_ratio (platform knob): reserve N extra warm slots per X active sessions (costly for low-util customers; useful for enterprise SLOs).
4) pack_threshold_tokens (runtime): don't schedule a new slot for batch < T tokens if an active slot can accept them within next Y ms. Tunable to avoid fragmentation.
5) early-first-byte-streaming flag: trade streaming granularity vs packing; enable when long-turns are dominant.

Recommended default config (console + SDK quickstart):
- SDK: client_side_buffer_ms = 25, multiplexer_per_conn = 2 (safe default), streaming_chunk_ms = 100
- Console: expose "interactive" profile that sets prewarm_reservation_ratio = 1 per 80 sessions for paid tiers; warns on small free-tier accounts.

Quick reproduction steps (local):
- Setup: single r4-equivalent GPU instance (use perf image), model: mid-sized causal model (~7B), token budget: short/long mix as above.
- Traffic generator: reuse bench-client V2 (bench-client --clients 400 --mix short:70,long:30 --iat-dist exp(mean=15ms) --buffer-ms <X>)
- Measure: aggregate with bench-collector (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, per-batch size histogram). Capture server traces for slot assignment events.

Risk and open questions:
- UX tradeoffs: some real-time voice agents may be intolerant of added buffer. Need micro-A/B on sample of users (we saw measurable sensation thresholds between 30–70ms in internal UX tests).
- Cost allocation: prewarm improves tail but creates idle cost; need billing signals to surface this to customers and toggleable console options.
- Multiplexer support across HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 vs websockets needs standardization—SDK changes alone are not sufficient.

Notes for next experiment:
- Run same matrix with multimodal requests (image+text). Hypothesis: multimodal long-turns shift sweet spot lower (smaller buffer needed) because per-request compute is higher so overhead amortization is better.
- Evaluate pack_threshold_tokens at different model sizes; threshold likely scales with kernel startup cost (bigger models -> larger threshold).

Suggested deliverables for Q1:
- Finalize console "interactive" profile and add an "optimize for tail" toggle (product + billing doc).
- SDK patch to add client_side_buffer_ms and multiplexing helpers; default enabled for new SDK minor release.
- Benchmark suite addition: bench-client scenarios for ping-penalty with automated p99 regressions.

Appendix: raw sample trace excerpt (simplified):
[trace snippet]
T=00:01:03.212 slot-assigned slot-7 batch-size=3 kernel-start=6ms kernel-compute=14ms
T=00:01:03.224 slot-assigned slot-8 batch-size=1 kernel-start=7ms kernel-compute=5ms (cold)
T=00:01:03.236 pack-merge attempt: slot-7 accepted +2 requests

Acknowledgements / owners: runtime: @luis (tracking pack_threshold), sdk: @sana (client buffering & multiplexing helpers), console: @ethan (profile UI + billing knob).

Open todo (short):
- Run 24h stability run for chosen default (25ms buffer) across 3 regions.
- Add a console tip with a one-click "enable interactive prewarm" for enterprise.
- Draft billing/FAQ language for prewarm idle charges.

End of draft.
